title: C# Complete Cheat Sheet
description: Comprehensive quick reference covering C# fundamentals, OOP, SOLID principles, design patterns, generics, async/await, collections, LINQ, and common interview topics.

data.text: Variables & Data Types

C# provides a rich set of value and reference types. Use the right type for the job: int for whole numbers, double for floating-point, decimal for financial calculations, string for text, and bool for true/false.

data.title: Primitive Types and var
Nullable Types
String Interpolation and Verbatim Strings

data.text: Operators
Operators perform operations on variables and values. C# supports arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment, and special null-aware operators introduced in recent versions.

data.title: Arithmetic and Comparison Operators
Logical and Ternary Operators

data.text: Control Flow
Control flow structures let you direct program execution. C# supports traditional if/else, switch statements, and modern switch expressions alongside loops for iteration.

data.title: If/Else and Switch
Switch Expression (C# 8+)
Loops: for, foreach, while, do-while
Break and Continue

data.text: Methods
Methods encapsulate reusable logic. C# supports reference parameters, optional and named arguments, expression-bodied members, and local functions for inline helpers.

data.title: Parameters: ref, out, in, Optional, Named
Expression-Bodied Members and Local Functions

data.text: Classes & Objects
Classes are blueprints for objects. They encapsulate data (fields) and behavior (methods). Modern C# supports auto-properties, init-only setters, and concise syntax for common patterns.

data.title: Class Definition, Constructors, Properties
The this Keyword

data.text: Inheritance

Inheritance allows a derived class to reuse and extend a base class. Use protected for members accessible in derived classes, sealed to prevent further inheritance, and base to call the parent implementation.

data.title: Base/Derived Classes and Protected Members
Sealed Classes and Methods

data.text: Interfaces
Interfaces define contracts that classes implement. They support multiple inheritance of behavior, explicit implementation to avoid name collisions, and default interface methods (C# 8+).

data.title: Interface Definition and Implementation
Explicit Interface Implementation

data.text: Access Modifiers
Access modifiers control visibility and accessibility. Choose the most restrictive modifier that satisfies your design needs.

data.title: Access Modifiers Overview

data.text: Records (C# 9)
Records provide built-in value equality, immutability support, and concise syntax for data-carrying types. Use them for DTOs, API responses, and immutable data models.

data.title: Record Classes and Positional Records
Record Structs

data.text: Tuples
Tuples group multiple values without creating a dedicated class. Named tuples improve readability, and deconstruction lets you unpack values cleanly.

data.title: ValueTuple Syntax and Named Tuples
Tuples as Return Values

data.text: Pattern Matching
Pattern matching lets you test values against shapes, types, and properties. It makes is expressions, switch statements, and switch expressions more expressive.

data.title: is Expressions and Type Patterns
Property and Positional Patterns
Relational Patterns

data.text: Exception Handling
Exception handling separates error handling from normal logic. Use specific exception types, exception filters for conditional catching, and throw expressions for concise validation.

data.title: Try/Catch/Finally and Throw Expressions

data.text: Async & Await
Async programming enables non-blocking I/O operations. Use async/await for readability, Task<T> for return values, and ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries.

data.title: Async Methods and Task<T>
Async Streams (IAsyncEnumerable<T>)

data.text: Delegates
Delegates are type-safe function pointers. Use Func, Action, and Predicate for common patterns, or define custom delegates for specific signatures.

data.title: Action, Func, Predicate, and Custom Delegates

data.text: Events
Events implement the publish-subscribe pattern. Publishers raise events, subscribers handle them. Use EventHandler<T> for type-safe event data.

data.title: Event Declaration and EventHandler<T>

data.text: Generics
Generics enable type-safe code reuse. Use them for classes, methods, structs, and interfaces. Constraints restrict what types can be used.

data.title: Generic Classes, Methods, and Constraints
Covariance and Contravariance

data.text: Collections
C# provides rich collection types. Use List<T> for ordered lists, Dictionary<K,V> for key-value pairs, Queue<T> for FIFO, Stack<T> for LIFO, and HashSet<T> for unique items.

data.title: List<T> and Dictionary<TKey, TValue>
Queue<T>, Stack<T>, and HashSet<T>
Collection Expressions (C# 12+)

data.text: LINQ Basics

Language Integrated Query (LINQ) provides a unified syntax for querying data from objects, databases, XML, and more. Use method syntax for complex operations and query syntax for SQL-like readability.

data.title: LINQ Method Syntax vs Query Syntax
Where, Select, OrderBy, and ThenBy

data.text: LINQ Advanced
Advanced LINQ operations enable complex data transformations including grouping, joining, flattening, and aggregation across multiple data sources.

data.title: GroupBy, Join, and GroupJoin
SelectMany, Zip, and Aggregate
Any, All, First, and Single

data.text: SOLID Principles
SOLID is a set of five design principles that make software more maintainable, flexible, and understandable.

data.title: S - Single Responsibility Principle
O - Open/Closed Principle
L - Liskov Substitution Principle
I - Interface Segregation Principle
D - Dependency Inversion Principle

data.text: Dependency Injection

Dependency Injection (DI) inverts control of creating dependencies. In .NET, the built-in DI container manages service lifetimes: Transient (new each time), Scoped (per request), and Singleton (one instance).

data.title: Constructor Injection and Service Lifetimes
Service Lifetimes: Transient, Scoped, Singleton

data.text: Common Design Patterns
Design patterns are reusable solutions to common problems. Below are six essential patterns every C# developer should know.
Singleton
Ensures only one instance exists. Use thread-safe lazy initialization.

data.title: Singleton Pattern

data.text: Factory
Creates objects without specifying exact classes. Encapsulates object creation logic.

data.title: Factory Pattern

data.text: Strategy
Defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each, and makes them interchangeable.

data.title: Strategy Pattern

data.text: Observer
Defines a one-to-many dependency so when one object changes state, all dependents are notified.

data.title: Observer Pattern with Events

data.text: Decorator
Attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically without affecting other objects of the same class.

data.title: Decorator Pattern

data.text: Repository
Mediates between the domain and data mapping layers, acting like an in-memory collection of domain objects.

data.title: Repository Pattern

data.text: Reflection
Reflection lets you inspect and manipulate types at runtime. Use it for serialization, dependency injection, and dynamic object creation.

data.title: Type Inspection and Activator.CreateInstance
Custom Attributes

data.text: File I/O
C# provides synchronous and asynchronous file operations. Use System.Text.Json for modern JSON serialization instead of older libraries.

data.title: File.ReadAllText and StreamReader
StreamWriter and Path Operations
JSON Serialization with System.Text.Json
